name: Umbugarla
confidence_why: Every description of Umbugarla stress goes back to one source, Davies 1989 (a BA Honours sketch grammar), whose statement of penultimate primary stress with a secondary stress on the first syllable is quoted verbatim in Goedemans 2010 and coded the same way in Goedemans 1998 and van der Hulst, Goedemans and Rice 2017, with no contrary source but with Davies herself noting many exceptions that carry initial main stress.

An overview of word stress in Australian Aboriginal languages. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton, p.72 (Google Books id AZGUEQmFqfMC, legacy volumes-feed excerpt, pg=PA72). Corroborated by Goedemans, Rob W.N. 1998. Weightless Segments. PhD diss., Leiden, Appendix D p.245 (open text) and by van der Hulst, Harry, Rob Goedemans & Keren Rice. 2017. Word prominence and areal linguistics. catalog_locator: Goedemans 2010: 72 with footnote 10 (quoting Davies 1989: 29). Corroboration: Goedemans 1998, Appendix D p.245 (category IV; code legend pp.235-236); van der Hulst, Goedemans & Rice 2017, Table 7.1 p.188 and p.190.
catalog_quote: Davies (1989: 29) describes the stress pattern of Umbugarla, spoken on the northwestern fringe of the penultimate stress area, as: " The basic pattern in Umbugarla is for primary stress to be located on the penultimate syllable of the word . Secondary stress is located on the first syllable . " 10 As in Waanji, we only have to set the Rhythm Iterative parameter in (22) to N (o) to derive this pattern . A fact that Davies also mentions with respect to Umbugarla is that there are many exceptions that have initial main stress . In an area that is as diffusionally active as Arnhem Land, such exceptions can be highly instrumental in our search to answer the question in which direction the stress patterns are evolving, especially if all the exceptions in a particular language have one single stress type . || Goedemans 1998 App. D p.245: "IV Stress is on the penultimate syllable: ... Umbugarla (T116) (E) (Ed): Davies, Jennifer (1989). Umbugarla: A sketch grammar. Honours Thesis, ANU." || van der Hulst, Goedemans & Rice 2017 Table 7.1 p.188: "R/tr | LR/tr Primary stress on the penult and only one secondary stress on the first. Umbugarla (Davies 1989) no example available"; p.190: "Example (25b), however, reveals the Umbugarla pattern, with only one secondary stress located on the left-hand side."

Honours Thesis, ANU.'), which is the last entry before the '246 AUSTRALIAN ABORIGINAL LANGUAGES' running head, i.e. printed p.245 of Appendix D; I re-extracted the PDF with extracted text and got the identical line. The code legend on p.235-236 (lines 10404-10418) reads 'E: the descriptive source notes many exceptions to the general rule' and 'Ed: 1 secondary stress is located at the edge opposite of main…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; a secondary stress falls on the word-initial syllable. The source reports many lexical exceptions with initial main stress instead.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable (Davies as quoted); Goedemans codes this 'Ed' (secondary stress at the edge opposite main stress); the 2017 Cambridge Handbook table phrases it as 'secondary stress on the first and alternates after it' but notes no example is available.
new_statements.exceptions: 'many exceptions that have initial main stress' (Goedemans 2010 reporting Davies); Goedemans 1998 code 'E' = descriptive source notes many exceptions to the general rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word domain ('of the word'); based on a salvage sketch grammar from limited recordings (Breen/Evans material); no information on phrase-level prosody or citation-form effects visible in the accessible snippets.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to Umbugarla proper (umbu1235; Tindale T116), as described by Davies 1989 from Breen/Evans recordings; Harvey 1992 notes the language name also covered Ngomburr (Ngurmbur) and possibly Bugurnidja, for which no separate data are attested (Glottolog comment). No dialect distinction is made in the stress statement.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's penultimate primary stress and with the Davies 1989 quotation (via Goedemans 2010) that secondary stress is on the first syllable; refines by making explicit that the secondary stress is a single non-iterative one and by placing the system in the hybrid typology. Grant, 'The Western Micronesian Sprachbund', ch. 30 (pp. 852ff) of the same Hickey volume, i.e. the WRONG chapter for this cita…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable; a single, non-iterative secondary stress falls on the first syllable (StressTyp parameters: primary domain right-edge trochee, secondary domain left-edge trochee, non-iterative). The chapter classifies this as an Arnhem Land 'hybrid' system between true initial-stress and true penultimate-stress languages, citing only Davies 1989 and giving no example word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: One secondary stress on the initial syllable only; explicitly NON-iterative (LR/tr without the asterisk), contrasted in the same table with Nunggubuyu (R/tr | LR*/tr: 'secondary stress on the first and alternates after it').
new_statements.exceptions: No Umbugarla-specific statement. Footnote 25 (p.187) says languages in this diffusionally active area 'will have scores of exceptions to regular patterns', and Section 7.7.3 (p.189-190) treats abundant exceptions as a sign of instability of the hybrid patterns, but the chapter does not repeat Goedemans 2010's remark that Umbugarla has many exceptions with initial main stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Umbugarla as a single variety, citing only Davies 1989 (Umbugarla: A Sketch Grammar); the 2017 chapter places it among Arnhem Land languages on the fringe of the penultimate-stress area. No dialect is named. The Edge Hill file at the listed open_url is a different chapter of the same handbook (Grant, Western Micronesian Sprachbund) and says nothing about Umbugarla.

new_statements.quote: The non-iterative rhythm variant of this pattern, that was embodied in Waanji in the other camp, can also be found among the penultimate stress languages. Davies (1989: 29) describes the stress pattern of Umbugarla, spoken on the northwestern fringe of the penultimate stress area, as: ''The basic pattern in Umbugarla is for primary stress to be located on the penultimate syllable of the word. Secondary stress is located on the first syllable.''10 As in Waanji, we only have to set the Rhythm Iterative parameter in (22) to N(o) to derive this pattern. A fact that Davies also mentions with respect to Umbugarla is that there are many exceptions that have initial main stress. [fn.10:] To make absolutely sure there is only one secondary stress, one should check whether the third syllable of six syllable words is stressed or not. Unfortunately, I did not find sufficiently long examples in Davies (1989).

Secondary stress is located on the first syllable."10 As in Waanji, we only have to set the…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (fixed penultimate; penultimate stress) and as both existing statements; this is the primary text behind existing statement 1, now read on the page (p.72) rather than from a Google Books snippet, so the page locator is confirmed. It adds: (i) one non-iterative secondary stress on the initial syllable, (ii) many lexical exceptions with initial main stress, (iii) the caveat that the non-iterative secondary cannot be verified from Davies' data. Nothing contradicts the catalog; the initial-stress exceptions are described as exceptions to a penultimate basic pattern, not as the pattern itself.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word; a single (non-iterative) secondary stress on the first syllable; StressTyp parameters as for Nunggubuyu in (22) (Stress Domain R, Rhythm Direction L, trochaic) but with Rhythm Iterative = No. Also on p.65 Umbugarla (Davies 1989) is listed among the Arnhem Land languages that 'have main stress on the penultimate syllable as their predominant stress pattern'. All of it is second-hand from Davies 1989: 29; no Umbugarla word forms are cited anywhere in the chapter.
new_statements.secondary_stress: One secondary stress on the first syllable (per Davies 1989: 29 as quoted). Goedemans notes in fn.10 that whether there is really only ONE secondary stress (i.e. non-iterative rhythm) cannot be verified because Davies gives no six-syllable examples in which a third-syllable secondary could be checked.
new_statements.exceptions: 'there are many exceptions that have initial main stress' (p.72, attributed to Davies 1989). Footnote 6 (p.66) says more generally that most of the Arnhem Land languages in figure 1 'have scores of exceptions with, sometimes even regularised, antepenultimate or initial stress'. Section 3.1 'Exceptional patterns' (pp.73ff.) does not return to Umbugarla specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: The chapter treats Umbugarla as a single language 'spoken on the northwestern fringe of the penultimate stress area' of Arnhem Land (figure 1, no. 20); no dialect is named. Umbugarla is extinct; Davies 1989 is the only primary description cited.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on primary stress placement: the catalog (penult), Goedemans 1998 App. D category IV, Goedemans 2010 quoting Davies 1989:29, and van der Hulst, Goedemans & Rice 2017 Table 7.1 all give penultimate primary stress with a secondary stress on the initial syllable. One internal correction: the earlier Google Books search-within snippet of the 2017 chapter rendered the Umbugarla row as 'secondary stress on the first and alternates after it'; the full proof shows that description belongs to the Nunggubuyu row (LR*/tr, iterative), while Umbugarla is 'only one secondary stress on the first' (LR/tr, non-iterative), which matches Goedemans 1998's 'Ed' code. Goedemans 2010 (snippet) reports many exceptions with initial main stress; the 2017 chapter says nothing Umbugarla-specific about exceptions, which is a silence, not a contradiction. The primary source, Davies 1989 (BA Hons thesis, Melbourne), remains unobtained; every statement is second-hand from it.
